title: Running TypeScript on Node
bridge: A Node project is like your frontend's package.json without the bundler: tsx runs .ts files directly, the way Vite does in dev. Except: nothing rewrites your imports. ES module rules apply exactly as written, so the package says "type": "module" and relative imports end in .js.
intro: Every service in ai-agents is TypeScript running on Node 24, outside the browser. This lesson sets up the shape they all share. That means ES modules, a strict tsconfig, tsx and tsc, npm workspaces and exact pins. You build it in ~/p1-lab, the folder every p1 lesson keeps growing.

picture.caption: One source tree, two tools: tsx runs it now, tsc checks it and builds dist/ for images.

steps.text: "type": "module" makes every file an ES module: import and export
in dev and in tests, tsx removes the types and runs the file at once
tsc reads the strict NodeNext rules
tsc checks every type; with --noEmit it only checks
a build writes plain .js files to dist/
an image runs node dist/main.js, with no TypeScript tools inside

p: Make a folder outside fcp. npm init writes a package.json. Two npm pkg set commands make it an ES module package that nobody can publish by mistake.
The .npmrc file sets save-exact, so npm writes 5.9.3 into package.json instead of ^5.9.3. Then we install the three dev tools at the versions the ai-agents repo pins.
sections.because: We pin exact versions, like Byte does, so a version only moves when a PR changes the lockfile.

code.text:
mkdir ~/p1-lab && cd ~/p1-lab
npm init -y > /dev/null
npm pkg set type=module
npm pkg set private=true --json
printf 'save-exact=true\n' > .npmrc
npm install -D typescript@5.9.3 tsx@4.20.3 @types/node@24.12.2

notes.text: Every .js file in this package is now an ES module: import, never require.
--json stores true as a boolean. npm refuses to publish a private package.
From now on every npm install writes an exact version, with no ^ or ~.
TypeScript 5.9 (the same line as Byte), tsx to run .ts files, and Node 24's type definitions.

sections.ifInstead: If instead you see 'EBADENGINE' or odd syntax errors later, check node --version prints v24.x and run nvm use 24.

p: An ES module (ESM) is a file that uses import and export. Node decides per package: "type": "module" means ESM. The Agent SDK, Temporal and our services are all ESM.

With NodeNext rules, a relative import must name the file Node will load at run time. After the build, greet.ts becomes greet.js, so you write ./greet.js even though the file in src/ is greet.ts. A workspace package is imported by its name, with no path.
sections.because: We write the .js ending because Node loads exactly the path in the import, and no bundler adds it.

notes.text: A named export. Our style is arrow functions with explicit return types.
Resolved through node_modules/@lab/shared, a link npm workspaces make (below).
The ending names the built file. Without it, tsc stops with error TS2835.
Top-level code runs when the module loads. In ESM you may also await at the top level.

sections.ifInstead: If instead tsc says 'TS2835: Relative import paths need explicit file extensions ... Did you mean './greet.js'?', add .js to the import.

p: The ai-agents repo has one tsconfig.base.json at the root, and each package extends it. Ours is the same.
svc/tsconfig.json adds four things: extends ../tsconfig.base.json, outDir dist, rootDir src, and include ["src"].
sections.because: We share one base config so every package follows the same module rules.

notes.text: All strict checks on, like the frontend: no implicit any, null checks.
The JavaScript version tsc writes. Node 24 runs all of it.
NodeNext follows Node's own rules: the package type decides ESM, and imports need endings.
A type-only import must say import type. tsc then never guesses which imports to drop.
Load Node's types (process, Buffer, node:fs) and nothing from the DOM.

sections.h: tsx runs, tsc checks and builds
p: tsx removes the types from a .ts file and runs it. It is fast because it never checks a type. We use it for dev runs and for every test (lesson p1-6).
tsc is the TypeScript compiler. tsc --noEmit checks every type and writes nothing; CI runs it as typecheck. tsc without --noEmit writes .js files to dist/, and a Docker image runs node dist/main.js.
sections.because: We keep both tools because tsx is fast but blind to types, and tsc finds the type errors.

notes.text: In ai-agents the names are @rhinohealth/ai-agents-<pkg>, such as @rhinohealth/ai-agents-broker.
-p points tsc at this package's tsconfig, which extends the base.
The same check with no output. CI runs this in the lint job.
Runs the built file. The gateway image does the same with CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"].
A dependency on the workspace package. npm links it instead of downloading it.

sections.h: npm workspaces: many packages, one lockfile
p: The root package.json lists the workspace folders. One npm install then installs everything into one node_modules and links each workspace there by its name. There is one package-lock.json for the whole repo.

-w runs a command in one workspace: npm install -w shared zod@4.6.7 adds zod to shared only. --workspaces --if-present runs a script in every package that has it. ai-agents has six workspaces at the start: shared, gateway, broker, orchestrator, harness and slack-app.
sections.because: We use one workspace because one lockfile, one install and one CI keep six packages from drifting apart.

notes.text: The name other packages import. It matches the dependency in svc/package.json.
Each package says its own type. Leaving it out would make shared CommonJS.
What import "@lab/shared" loads. Here it is the .ts source; tsx and tsc both read it.

callout.text: node svc/dist/main.js also loads shared/src/index.ts. Node 24 removes simple types from .ts files on its own (check the Node docs for 'type stripping'), but only outside node_modules. The workspace link points at your folder, so it works here. Real images run built or bundled code.

p: npm install may update the lockfile. npm ci never does: it deletes node_modules, installs exactly what the lockfile says, and fails if package.json and the lockfile disagree. CI and Docker builds always use npm ci.
Some packages run scripts on install. --ignore-scripts turns those off, so a hijacked dependency cannot run code during the build. Byte's images and ours install with npm ci --ignore-scripts.
sections.because: We use npm ci --ignore-scripts in builds, so a build is the exact lockfile and runs no code we never read.

code.text:
npm install -w shared zod@4.6.7   # adds "zod": "4.6.7" to shared, no ^
grep zod shared/package.json
npm ci --ignore-scripts           # what CI and Dockerfiles run

notes.text: Installs into the shared workspace. We use zod there in lesson p1-5.
Proof that save-exact worked.
Wipes node_modules and installs the lockfile exactly, running no install scripts.

sections.ifInstead: If instead npm ci says the package.json and package-lock.json are not in sync, run npm install once. Then commit the lockfile.

quiz.q: svc/src/main.ts imports "./greet" and tsc fails with TS2835. What is the fix?

options.why: tsc refuses a .ts ending unless you turn on allowImportingTsExtensions, and Node would then load the wrong file after the build.
NodeNext wants the name of the file that runs after the build.

options.text: Set moduleResolution to node so endings are optional
options.why: That hides the problem from tsc; Node still needs the ending at run time. We keep NodeNext like Byte.

quiz.q: tsx runs a file that has a type error. What happens?

options.text: tsx refuses to run it and prints the error
options.why: tsx never checks types; it only removes them.

options.text: It runs; only tsc (typecheck) reports the error
options.why: That is why CI runs npm run typecheck on every PR.

options.text: It runs, and the bad value becomes undefined
options.why: Types do not exist at run time, so nothing is changed in the values.

quiz.q: Why do CI and our Dockerfiles run npm ci instead of npm install?

options.text: npm ci installs exactly the lockfile and fails if package.json disagrees with it
options.why: A build must be repeatable; npm install may quietly update the lockfile.

options.text: npm ci is faster because it skips the lockfile
options.why: It does the opposite: the lockfile is the only thing it follows.

options.text: npm ci updates every package to its latest patch version

words.plain: A JavaScript file that uses import and export; "type": "module" makes every file in a package one.
The tsconfig module rules that follow Node exactly; relative imports need their .js ending.
A tool that removes types from .ts files and runs them, without checking types.
The TypeScript compiler: checks types, and with a build writes .js files to dist/.
Several packages in one repo with one node_modules and one lockfile, linked by name.
A dependency written as 4.6.7, not ^4.6.7, so only a lockfile change moves it.
Installs exactly the lockfile and fails if package.json disagrees; used in CI and images.

tickets.why: Creates ai-agents with this exact shape: ESM, NodeNext, npm workspaces, tsx, tsc and exact pins.
The gateway is the first workspace with real code: gateway/src/server.ts built by tsc.

remember: ESM with .js endings, a strict NodeNext tsconfig, tsx to run, tsc to check, one lockfile, exact pins.
